# Chapter 5 — The Exit Criteria — When Azure Native Takes Full Ownership

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
Retiring the third-party DDI platform is the conclusion of a verifiable sequence, not a single event. This chapter defines the four exit criteria the environment must satisfy before retirement can begin — zone completion, DHCP scope migration, forwarder removal, and a final reconciliation — then walks the operational retirement procedure: read-only mode, the thirty-day monitoring window, and appliance decommission. It closes with what the OrgPath model leaves behind once the bridge platform is gone.
:::

## The Four Exit Criteria

Retiring the third-party DDI platform is not a single event — it is the conclusion of a sequence of verifiable conditions, each of which must be confirmed before the next step proceeds. The platform has been the system of record for the organization's DNS and IP address estate, in some cases for a decade or more, and its retirement cannot be treated as a routine infrastructure decommission. The exit criteria below define the state the environment must reach before the retirement sequence can begin. They are organized around the same Decommissioning Readiness Score framework introduced in Part Eight, extended here to account for the additional surface area introduced by the third-party DDI platform.

> No criterion is advisory. Each one, until it is met, represents a live resolution or addressing path still served from the platform — and retiring the platform with any criterion outstanding would break that path.

The four criteria, and the mechanism that verifies each, are summarized below.

| # | Exit criterion | Required state | Verification mechanism |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | **Zone completion** | Every zone authoritative in the NIOS Grid or BlueCat DNS View carries `MigrationPhase = Complete` and has a matching Azure DNS Private Zone (tagged with the OrgPath value, linked to the hub VNet, reachable from the resolver inbound endpoint) | Reconciliation script (Chapter Four): zero NIOS-only zones, zero Azure-only zones lacking a Complete-phase NIOS entry, zero phase mismatches |
| 2 | **DHCP scope migration** | Every DDI-managed scope has an explicit disposition — either absorbed into Azure VNet address space, or migrated to Windows Server DHCP under the IPAM role with the failover relationship verified and the DDI scope record marked decommissioned | Governance log: no active DDI scope left without a recorded migration disposition |
| 3 | **Forwarder removal** | No conditional forwarding rule on the Azure DNS Private Resolver Forwarding Ruleset references any NIOS or BAM name-server IP address | Final check confirms zero forwarding rules pointing at DDI name servers |
| 4 | **Final reconciliation** | The Chapter-Four reconciliation script reports zero NIOS-only, zero Azure-only, and zero phase-mismatch entries; the fully-synchronized count equals the total zones formerly in the DDI platform | Archived reconciliation report in the governance repository — the definitive completion record |

**Criterion 1 — Zone completion** is a hard requirement: the existence of even a single zone in the Assessment, Migration, or Parallel state means some DNS resolution is still being served from the DDI platform, and retiring it would cause resolution failures for clients that depend on those zones. The reconciliation script from Chapter Four is the mechanism that verifies it, and all three of its delta categories must read zero before the criterion is considered met.

**Criterion 2 — DHCP scope migration** turns on a single principle: no DHCP scope that was active in the DDI platform can be left without an explicit migration disposition in the governance record. Either the address range the scope served has been absorbed into Azure Virtual Network address space — meaning all hosts that formerly received dynamic addresses from the on-premises scope are now Azure-hosted and receive assignments through Azure's built-in DHCP mechanism — or the scope has been migrated to a Windows Server DHCP server managed through the Windows Server IPAM role described in Part Eight, with the failover relationship to its partner verified and the DDI scope record marked decommissioned. A scope simply deleted from the DDI platform without being migrated represents an address management gap that may not surface immediately but will cause lease conflicts or addressing failures later.

**Criterion 3 — Forwarder removal** targets configuration inconsistency. A forwarding rule for a zone whose NIOS or BAM counterpart has been marked Complete means the zone is fully hosted in Azure DNS, yet the resolver is still forwarding queries for it to an on-premises name server that is no longer authoritative — which, in an active system, causes resolution failures for those queries.

> Remove the forwarding rule for each zone *as* its `MigrationPhase` advances to Complete — not at the end of the entire migration. Doing so validates the Complete state in real time and lets the resolver configuration converge incrementally rather than all at once.

The final check before retirement is simply confirming that no forwarding rules remain that reference any of the DDI platform's name-server addresses.

**Criterion 4 — Final reconciliation** runs the Chapter-Four reconciliation script one last time. Its output must show zero entries in the NIOS-only, Azure-only, and phase-mismatch categories, and the fully-synchronized count must equal the total number of zones previously managed in the DDI platform — confirming that every zone has been accounted for in Azure DNS and that none was lost during the migration. This report is archived in the governance repository as the definitive migration completion record.

## The Operational Retirement Procedure

Once all four exit criteria have been verified, the retirement procedure begins. It proceeds in three stages: read-only transition, a thirty-day monitoring window, and final decommission.

1. **Place the DDI platform in read-only mode.** In Infoblox NIOS, this is accomplished through the Grid's access control system: the service account used by the governance pipeline and the day-to-day DNS administration accounts are demoted to read-only roles, removing the ability to create, modify, or delete any DNS record, zone, or network object in the Grid. The Grid Master interface remains accessible for monitoring and audit-log queries but accepts no write operations. In BlueCat Address Manager, the equivalent is achieved through the BAM access control mechanism, setting all non-administrative user accounts to read-only access at the Configuration level. The network operations team is notified of the read-only transition and advised that any DNS or IPAM changes arising during the monitoring window must be made through Azure-native tooling — the Azure portal, the `Az.PrivateDns` module, or the governance pipeline — rather than through the DDI platform interface.

2. **Observe the thirty-day monitoring window.** The window runs thirty calendar days from the date of the read-only transition. During this period, DNS query logs from the Azure DNS Private Resolver are the primary monitoring artifact. The resolver logs — streamed to an Azure Monitor Log Analytics workspace through the diagnostic settings on the resolver resource — are queried daily to verify that no queries are being forwarded to the DDI platform's name-server IP addresses. A query that reaches the resolver and matches no local Azure DNS Private Zone would normally generate a SERVFAIL or NXDOMAIN response; if such responses appear at a rate higher than baseline during the window, the resolution path for those queries must be traced to determine whether they represent a forwarding rule missed during cleanup or a client configuration bypassing the resolver entirely and querying the old DDI platform name servers directly.

3. **Decommission the appliances.** If the thirty-day window passes without any forwarded queries to the DDI platform's name servers, the Grid Master or BAM appliances are decommissioned following the organization's standard server decommission procedure. The virtual machines or physical appliances are powered off, snapshots are taken for archive purposes, and the licenses are returned to the vendor. The governance repository receives a final commit recording the retirement date in ISO 8601 format, the path to the final reconciliation report, the names of the engineers who performed the verification steps, and the names of the approvers who authorized the retirement. This commit message becomes the permanent record of the DDI platform's lifecycle within the OrgPath governance model.

Every OrgTree node whose `MigrationPhase` field has not already been updated to Complete during the zone-by-zone migration sequence is updated in this final commit. From this point forward, the `MigrationPhase` field in the OrgTree registry is a historical attribute — it records the migration state at the time of retirement, not an active governance control. The active governance controls for DNS and IP address management are now entirely the Azure DNS Private Zones, the Azure Virtual Network address-space assignments, and the Azure DNS Private Resolver forwarding configuration, all of which carry OrgPath tags set and maintained by the same governance pipeline that formerly wrote to the DDI platform's REST API. The pipeline target list shrinks by one entry: the DDI platform's API endpoint is removed, and the pipeline routes all DNS and IPAM governance operations to Azure-native APIs.

## What the DDI Platform Leaves Behind

The third-party DDI platform's role in the OrgPath architecture was always defined by its temporality. It was a bridge — a system of record that maintained visibility and operational control during the period when neither the on-premises Active Directory-integrated DNS and DHCP nor the Azure-native DNS and virtual network address management was sufficient on its own to govern the full network estate. The bridge served its purpose:

- It **prevented IP address conflicts** by maintaining a unified address inventory.
- It **prevented DNS split-brain failures** by providing a single authoritative view of the zone inventory during the transition.
- It **supplied the audit trail and change workflow** that the organization's operational governance requirements demanded while two separate environments were managed simultaneously.

OrgPath was the thread that ran through the bridge. The same organizational context — the same node identifiers, the same hierarchy paths, the same tier classifications — that was encoded on Entra ID user objects, Intune device objects, Arc resource tags, and Microsoft Defender device groups was also encoded on NIOS zones and networks, on BlueCat zones and IP networks, and on Azure DNS Private Zones. Every system that touched a governed resource could answer the same question — what organizational context does this object belong to? — through its own native query interface, without any cross-system lookup.

> This is the value the OrgPath model provides that no individual system provides alone. When the bridge is retired, the organizational context does not retire with it.

It has already been propagated — zone by zone, network by network, device by device — to every Azure-native construct that carries organizational identity forward. The DDI platform leaves, and what remains is an environment where every DNS zone, every virtual network subnet, every resource tag, every device object, and every identity object carries the same coherent organizational context, expressed entirely through Azure-native mechanisms that require no additional platform to maintain. The OrgPath model has not changed. The substrate it runs on has converged, at last, to a single system — and the governance pipeline that enforces it runs lighter, faster, and with fewer moving parts than at any point during the transition. That convergence is what the entire hybrid migration was building toward, and the retirement of the DDI platform is the operational marker that confirms it has been reached.
